stories.headline: Thiruparankundram Karthigai Deepam lit at usual spot, not at pillar the Supreme Court allowed
stories.dek: The Madurai Collector had told the High Court he would comply with the Supreme Court order; BJP and Hindu groups protested while TVK allies backed the decision.
stories.summary: The Karthigai Deepam at Thiruparankundram in Madurai was lit on Tuesday at the traditional hilltop spot, not at the 'deepathoon' pillar the Supreme Court had allowed as a one-time arrangement. The BJP and Hindu groups accused the state government of defiance; the temple board cited custom.
body: The ceremonial Karthigai Deepam at Thiruparankundram in Madurai was lit at 6 pm on Tuesday at the customary Deepa Mandapam near the Uchipillayar temple, not at the 'deepathoon' pillar that the Supreme Court had permitted for this year.

On November 20, the Supreme Court allowed the lighting at the pillar as a one-time arrangement and said it would create no customary right to do so in later years. Earlier on Tuesday, the Madurai Bench of the Madras High Court recorded an undertaking by Madurai Collector Nishant Krishna that he would act in strict compliance with the Supreme Court's orders.

The district administration said in a statement that all arrangements were made as directed by the court. It said the temple Devasthanam was asked and reminded in writing to authorise its team, but did not do so until the last moment. Instead, the administration said, the temple's Board of Trustees passed a resolution to light the lamp at the usual place.

The Arulmigu Subramaniya Swamy Temple's Executive Officer, G. Selvi, and Board chairman V. Shanmugasundaram said in a joint press release that the temple followed age-old practice and agama rules. The board said the Deepa Mandapam lies directly above the head of the presiding deity. Law Minister C.T.R. Nirmal Kumar confirmed on social media that the lamp was lit there.

Police detained several BJP leaders, including state president Nainar Nagenthran, and members of Hindu outfits to stop them reaching the hill. Nagenthran said no legally valid prohibitory order existed. The Hindu reported that some protesters damaged buses and other public property. Detentions continued until 8 pm, after which devotees could walk the Girivalam path freely. Hindu Munnani said its state president, Kadeswara Subramaniam, was arrested in Tiruppur.

BJP leader Tamilisai Soundararajan called the law minister's stance 'highly condemnable' and demanded his removal. BJP general secretary B.L. Santhosh said the government had defied the court order. AIADMK general secretary Edappadi K Palaniswami said a government must abide by Supreme Court orders. K. Annamalai accused the government of acting arbitrarily and disregarding Supreme Court rulings.

TVK allies including the Congress, VCK, the Left parties and the MMK welcomed the decision. VCK president Thol Thirumavalavan thanked the Chief Minister, C. Joseph Vijay, for what he called thwarting a conspiracy and protecting social harmony.

According to Organiser, the High Court on Tuesday also said a pending state review petition was no ground for non-compliance. Heavy security remained at the hill late into the night, with access to the dargah and the deepathoon cordoned off.
keyFacts: The lamp was lit at 6 pm on Tuesday at the Deepa Mandapam near the Uchipillayar temple.
The Supreme Court allowed lighting at the deepathoon as a one-time arrangement on November 20.
Collector Nishant Krishna had told the Madras High Court he would comply with the order.
Police detained protesters and BJP leaders, including state president Nainar Nagenthran.
Congress, VCK, Left parties and MMK backed the government's decision.
stories.background: The Supreme Court's November 20 interim order allowed the lamp to be lit at the disputed stone pillar on Thiruparankundram hill this year only. The pillar is the subject of a dispute, and the hill also houses a dargah. The Tamil Nadu government has a review petition pending.
stories.whyItMatters: The episode sets the state government and its temple administration against an interim Supreme Court order, and the matter remains before the courts.

perspectives.summary: They say the government defied the Supreme Court and the High Court undertaking, ignored devotees' sentiments, and must be held accountable. The BJP says protests will continue until the lamp is lit at the pillar.

perspectives.summary: The temple board says it followed age-old custom and agama rules, and the administration says it asked the temple to authorise a team. Allies such as Congress, VCK and the Left say the decision protected tradition and social harmony.

stories.headline: US set to announce new tariffs on India and 15 other trading partners
stories.dek: The US Trade Representative's excess-capacity findings, due as soon as this week, would add duties on top of existing tariffs, people familiar with the plan said.
stories.summary: The Trump administration is preparing to release findings of a Section 301 probe into excess industrial capacity in 16 trading partners, including India, sources told Reuters. New duties would stack on existing tariffs, but rates and exemptions are unclear.
body: The Trump administration is preparing to publish the findings of a probe into alleged excess industrial capacity in 16 major trading partners, including India, with new import duties expected, three people with knowledge of the matter told Reuters on Tuesday.

The results of the investigation, conducted under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, could come as soon as Tuesday or Wednesday, the people said. The Wall Street Journal also reported that they could be unveiled this week. The US Trade Representative's office and the White House did not immediately respond to Reuters queries.

The USTR is expected to propose duties that would be added to tariffs already imposed during President Donald Trump's second term. The people said it was unclear what rates would apply or what exemptions might be granted. Business Standard, citing the Journal, reported that the final rates would be over and above existing ones.

The 16 economies are China, the European Union, India, Japan, South Korea, Mexico, Vietnam, Taiwan, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Switzerland, Norway, Singapore, Bangladesh and Cambodia. USTR Jamieson Greer has said subsidies and other government support created excess capacity that lets firms flood global markets with cheaper goods and undermine US producers, the Journal reported.

The administration has singled out China as the largest source of excess capacity, citing steel, aluminium, electric vehicles, appliances and solar products. China has rejected the accusation, saying its exports reflect competitive advantages. The probe is also partly aimed at Chinese investment in Vietnam, Indonesia and Cambodia to make goods for the US market and avoid tariffs.

For India, the duties arrive while it negotiates an interim bilateral trade agreement with the US. The framework the two sides finalised in February was reopened after the US Supreme Court struck down tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, Business Standard reported. India is seeking lower tariffs than competitors such as Bangladesh, Vietnam and Cambodia.
One of Reuters' sources said the 20% cap on second-term tariffs on Chinese goods would likely stay while the US-China trade truce is extended. The truce is due to expire on January 10.
keyFacts: The probe covers 16 economies, including India, China, the EU and Japan.
USTR opened the excess-capacity investigation on March 11, under Section 301.
In July, the US imposed 10% or 12.5% forced-labour duties on about 60 partners.
Rates and exemptions for the new duties have not been disclosed.
The US-China trade truce is due to expire on January 10.
stories.background:
The new duties would partly replace global tariffs struck down by the US Supreme Court in February. USTR launched the excess-capacity probe in March alongside a separate inquiry into lax enforcement of forced-labour laws in 59 countries and the EU, which led to the July duties.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll after November's midterm elections found 62% of respondents would support efforts to repeal the tariffs.
stories.whyItMatters: Additional US duties would raise costs for Indian exporters as New Delhi seeks better terms than rival suppliers such as Bangladesh, Vietnam and Cambodia in an interim trade deal.

stories.headline: Huang apologises to Nvidia staff, says he is in therapy
stories.dek: The reinstated chief executive told an all-hands meeting he broke a code of conduct he helped write, as Schumer and the attorney general's remarks kept scrutiny on him.
stories.summary: Jensen Huang told Nvidia staff on Tuesday he had made "terrible mistakes" and was in therapy, a day after his reinstatement as CEO. Shares fell about six percent after Monday's surge, and he faces congressional hearings next week.
body: Jensen Huang apologised to Nvidia staff at an all-hands meeting in Santa Clara, California, on Tuesday, saying he was in therapy and had made "terrible mistakes", a day after the company reinstated him as chief executive.

"I made some terrible mistakes," Huang said, according to The New York Times, which reviewed a livestream of the hourlong meeting. He told employees it was "not acceptable" that he had broken a code of conduct he had helped write. CNBC reported that he also said, "I hurt all of you."

Reuters, citing a source, reported that Huang said he had violated the code. He told staff it remained in force, but that mitigating circumstances would matter. Wired quoted him as saying it "does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door."

Huang resigned on November 12 over extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, according to the NDTV report. Nvidia said on Monday it had brought him back after receiving information from the US government that he did not pose a national security risk.

Huang thanked the Trump administration for quick access to intelligence that, he said, helped the board judge the risk to be low, The Wall Street Journal reported. He dismissed suggestions that Trump had pressured the board. Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had spoken to directors: "I spoke to them, let me put it that way. And I convinced them."

US Attorney General Todd Blanche, at an unrelated press conference in Washington on Tuesday, said: "Nvidia is a good corporate citizen." Al Jazeera reported that he declined to confirm whether Huang had been investigated, after Trump described a "thorough" probe. Reuters reported that Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer accused Huang of violating US export control law. The full details of Schumer's accusation were not available.
Nvidia shares, which rose more than 30 percent on Monday, closed about six percent lower on Tuesday. "The optimism faded quickly," Fawad Razaqzada of Forex.com wrote.
Huang is due before three House committees in a closed-door hearing on December 1 and a livestreamed Senate committee hearing on December 3.
keyFacts: Huang addressed Nvidia staff on Tuesday, a day after being reinstated as CEO.
He resigned on November 12 over extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy.
Nvidia shares rose over 30 percent on Monday and fell about six percent on Tuesday.
Closed-door House hearing is set for December 1; a Senate hearing for December 3.
stories.background: Nvidia's board is still running an internal investigation into concerns that Huang may have been the target of a Chinese espionage campaign, though Trump says he has been cleared. The Justice Department is separately investigating Singapore-based Megaspeed over alleged diversion of Nvidia processors to Chinese customers. The Securities and Exchange Commission has reportedly opened a probe into Nvidia's accounting and shareholder communications.
stories.whyItMatters: Nvidia's chips are central to AI investment, and its shares and those of linked firms fell sharply after Huang's resignation. Congressional scrutiny is expected to intensify in January, when Democrats take control of both chambers.

stories.headline: Akali Dal and BJP revive Punjab alliance for 2027 Assembly election
stories.dek: Home Minister Amit Shah said the Akali Dal would be the senior partner and claim the chief minister's post if the NDA wins; Congress called the tie-up desperate.
stories.summary: The Shiromani Akali Dal and the BJP announced on Tuesday that they will contest the Punjab Assembly election together, six years after the Akalis left the NDA over the farm laws. Seat-sharing details are yet to be announced.
body: The Shiromani Akali Dal and the Bharatiya Janata Party announced on Tuesday that they will fight the next Punjab Assembly election together, reviving an alliance that ended in 2020 over the farm laws.

Union Home Minister Amit Shah made the announcement at a press conference in New Delhi with SAD president Sukhbir Singh Badal and BJP chief Nitin Nabin. The date coincided with Guru Nanak's birth anniversary. The Times of India reported that Shah described the Akali Dal as the "big brother" in the alliance and the claimant to the chief minister's post if the NDA returns to office. No chief ministerial candidate was named.

Shah called the alliance "a symbol of Hindu-Sikh brotherhood", according to Scroll. He said that if elected, it would work to free Punjab of drugs and corruption and to strengthen nationalist forces in the state. He also said: "The alliance between BJP and SAD is not merely political; it is an emotional bond rooted in mutual trust and Punjab's history. NDA is now complete with Akali Dal's return."

Badal said: "A tidal wave has started today." He claimed the alliance would win 100 seats in the 117-member Assembly. Nabin said seat-sharing details would be announced later. The Times of India reported that the BJP is expected to contest more than the 23 seats it contested in earlier alliances.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi called it a "natural alliance". He is due to attend a rally in Moga on December 8 marking Parkash Singh Badal's birth anniversary. Modi had met Sukhbir Badal in the Parliament complex on August 7, which the Times of India described as the first clear sign of the tie-up.

Congress general secretary in charge of Punjab, Sachin Pilot, called it "a compromised alliance, a desperate alliance". He asked whether the Centre had given assurances on MSP or apologised for the farm laws, and what the SAD's view was on protesters who died during the farmers' protest. He said both parties had "no political space left in the state".

The Akalis left the NDA in 2020 over the three farm laws, since repealed. Harsimrat Kaur Badal resigned from the Union Cabinet that year. In 2022 the SAD, allied with the Bahujan Samaj Party, won three seats and the BJP won two. The Aam Aadmi Party won 92 seats and the Congress 18. The Assembly's term ends on March 16.
keyFacts: The SAD and BJP announced the alliance on Tuesday, Guru Nanak's birth anniversary.
The Akalis quit the NDA in 2020 over the farm laws.
In 2022 the SAD won three seats, the BJP two, AAP 92, Congress 18.
Sukhbir Badal claimed the alliance would win 100 of 117 seats.
Modi is due at a rally in Moga on December 8.
stories.background: The SAD and BJP governed Punjab together for a decade until 2017, when Congress won. The Akalis broke away in 2020 over farm laws that were later repealed. AAP won the state in 2022.
stories.whyItMatters: The tie-up makes the contest in Punjab potentially three-cornered between the SAD-BJP alliance, the governing AAP and the Congress ahead of polls expected early next year.

stories.headline: US jury convicts Huawei on 10 of 12 counts, clears it of racketeering conspiracy
stories.dek: Jurors in Brooklyn found the company guilty of trade-secret conspiracy and bank fraud but rejected the racketeering charge, the most serious it faced.
stories.summary: A federal jury in Brooklyn convicted Huawei Technologies on 10 of 12 counts on Tuesday, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets, bank fraud and sanctions violations. It acquitted the company of racketeering conspiracy; sentencing is planned for September 2027.
body: A federal jury in Brooklyn on Tuesday convicted Chinese technology company Huawei Technologies on 10 of 12 counts, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but acquitted it of racketeering conspiracy.

The convictions also include conspiracy to violate US sanctions, according to the BBC. The South China Morning Post reported that the counts included wire fraud and sanctions evasion, and that the jury also found Huawei not guilty of conspiracy to obstruct justice. The case involved Huawei and three subsidiaries.

The racketeering charge, under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act, required jurors to find that the company operated as a criminal enterprise. The BBC described it as the more serious, overarching charge.

Prosecutors argued during the two-month trial that Huawei lied, cheated and stole to gain a competitive edge. Assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors in closing arguments that the company spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand, including lying to banks about its Iran business and taking secrets from rivals. "The tone was set at the top by Huawei leaders and executives who themselves engaged in criminal conduct," she said.

The indictment alleged that Huawei sold routers containing source code copied from a competitor, and that a person working for Huawei photographed the circuits inside a rival's device at a Chicago trade show. Court records list Cisco Systems, Motorola Solutions, T-Mobile, Quintel USA and Fujitsu among the victim companies.

Huawei's defence lawyer, Brian Heberlig, said prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built their case from there. He told jurors the company succeeded through "hard work, innovation and competition", and said much of the material allegedly stolen was already public.

In a statement, Huawei said the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis and vindicates our consistent position over the past eight years". Heberlig told the BBC the racketeering count was "a significant overreach". He added: "Of course, we have mixed emotions about the rest of the verdict."

The BBC said it had contacted the US Department of Justice for comment. Chinese officials have said the US engages in "economic bullying" and uses national security as a pretext to oppress Chinese companies.
Heberlig said there will be "significant advocacy" for the lowest possible sentence, and that he fully expects Huawei to appeal. Sentencing is planned for September 2027.
keyFacts: The jury in Brooklyn convicted Huawei on 10 of 12 counts on Tuesday, November 24.
Huawei was acquitted of racketeering conspiracy and of conspiracy to obstruct justice.
The trial lasted two months; US charges were first announced in 2019.
Sentencing is planned for September 2027, and Huawei's lawyer expects an appeal.
stories.background:
US prosecutors announced charges against Huawei in early 2019, after the arrest in Canada in late 2018 of chief financial officer Meng Wanzhou, and later expanded the allegations. Meng returned to China in 2021 in a prisoner swap that freed two Canadians held by China, and the US dropped its case against her.

Huawei has not been allowed to sell equipment to US carriers for years over security concerns, and Canada and Britain have also restricted it. It still sells smartphones and telecom equipment globally and has expanded into chipmaking.
stories.whyItMatters: The verdict ends a case that began in 2019 and leaves Huawei facing sentencing next year. The Associated Press reported it is unclear what effect the outcome will have on the company's global fortunes.

stories.headline: CIA and ODNI discover breach of unclassified intelligence analysis system
stories.dek: Sources say no classified systems were affected and the issue has been resolved; it is unclear what data was exposed or who was responsible.
stories.summary: The CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence recently discovered a cyber breach that exposed unclassified information, the New York Times reported on Tuesday. Sources said no classified systems were hit and the issue has been resolved.
body: The US Central Intelligence Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) recently discovered a cyber breach that exposed some unclassified information, the New York Times reported on Tuesday, citing people familiar with the matter.

The intrusion affected a network used to find intelligence insights in public, unclassified material, the Times said. Fox News and the New York Post described it as an open-source intelligence analysis system. Information at other government agencies was also believed to have been exposed, the Times reported, citing a source.

A person familiar with the incident told The Associated Press, on condition of anonymity, that the breach involved no classified information and the issue had been resolved. Sources told Fox News the same. It was not clear what specific information was compromised or who was responsible.
The ODNI said there had been "no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems." The CIA declined the New York Post's request for comment and did not immediately respond to The Hindu's.

Open-source intelligence draws on publicly available data, including the internet, commercial satellites and private data brokers, according to the AP. Though the information is generally public or semi-public, it can give analysts significant insight on its own or combined with classified intelligence.

Fox News, citing multiple sources, reported that the CIA, the ODNI and the FBI were breached on the same day last week. It said it was unclear whether the intrusions were connected. Fox's Jennifer Griffin reported that the FBI breach was more serious because it affected the National Crime Information Center, a database law enforcement agencies use to share and look up information.

Two Pentagon officials told Fox News the Department of War was not breached. Griffin also reported that a separate outage hit an internal classified National Security Agency system for several days last week, and that it stemmed from an internal technology upgrade.

The Trump administration says the recent outages are not part of a coordinated cyberattack. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on Sunday news shows that the outages largely stem from the rush to patch and upgrade systems to stay ahead of hackers using sophisticated artificial intelligence tools, according to the AP.
keyFacts: The New York Times reported the breach on Tuesday, November 24, citing people familiar with the matter.
Sources say no classified systems were affected and the issue has been resolved.
The ODNI said there were no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems.
Fox News reported the CIA, ODNI and FBI were breached on the same day last week.
The data exposed and those responsible have not been identified.
stories.background: The report follows a series of system failures this month. A nationwide ground stop disrupted air travel, and Apple, JP Morgan Chase and Microsoft had systems go down. The FBI is investigating a hack of its national law enforcement database, and a breach was reported at the US Department of Agriculture. The Hindu reported two separate recent breaches at the FBI.
stories.whyItMatters: The incidents have drawn attention to vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure, banking systems and digital tools used by millions of people, according to the AP.

stories.headline: Nvidia falls after record rally as AI stocks pull Nasdaq down 1.45%
stories.dek: Anthropic closed below its $83 IPO price, while the Dow rose and Asian markets rebounded on the back of Monday's surge in chip stocks.
stories.summary: Nvidia shares fell on Tuesday, a day after their biggest one-day gain in over two decades, and AI-linked stocks pulled the Nasdaq down 1.45%. Anthropic slipped below its IPO price, while the Dow rose and Asian markets gained.
body: Nvidia and other AI-linked shares fell on Tuesday, giving back part of Monday's rally and pulling the Nasdaq Composite down 1.45% to 23,740.52 as Wall Street closed mixed.

The S&P 500 lost 34.72 points, or 0.48%, to 7,202.45. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 433.48 points, or 0.87%, to 50,028.79. Technology led declines in the S&P 500, according to The Economic Times.

Reports differed on the size of Nvidia's fall. Mint reported a drop of 9% to $150.50 in Tuesday trade, after a Monday close of $165.05. CNA said the stock fell almost 6%, and Business Standard put the decline at 4.7%. Monday's gain was reported as more than 30%, with Mint giving 31.48%.

Nvidia surged on Monday after its board reinstated founder Jensen Huang as chief executive. Huang had resigned earlier this month following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Mint said the rally added nearly $1 trillion to Nvidia's market value.

Anthropic fell 6.5% to $81.91, below the $83 price at which it listed last week, CNA reported. Hewlett Packard Enterprise fell 13% after guiding for weaker operating margins in its cloud and AI segment in fiscal 2027, Mint said, citing Bloomberg. Semiconductor stocks and CoreWeave also weakened.

Investors also weighed tariffs. Reuters, cited by The Economic Times, reported that the Trump administration is poised to release findings of a probe into alleged excess industrial capacity in 16 major trading partners, with new import duties expected.

"After the biggest rally in months, you would expect some profit-taking," said Gene Goldman, chief investment officer at Cetera Financial Group. "At the end of the day, one headline doesn't really resolve investor questions about the AI trade."

Peter Cardillo of Spartan Capital said the Nvidia episode was hitting one sector rather than the whole market. Merck, Nike, Amgen and Salesforce each gained more than 4%, CNA reported. Sanofi rose almost 10% after announcing a $41 billion purchase of Insmed.

Asian markets had risen earlier on Tuesday. Taipei gained 9%, Seoul more than 6% and Tokyo nearly 4%, according to CNA. MSCI's Asia Pacific index rose 1.5%, ending eight straight sessions of losses, Business Standard said.
Investors are awaiting Wednesday's Personal Consumption Expenditures price index. Traders mostly expect a 25-basis-point Fed rate increase next month, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool.
keyFacts: Nasdaq Composite fell 1.45% to 23,740.52 on Tuesday; the Dow rose 0.87% to 50,028.79.
Anthropic closed at $81.91, below its $83 IPO price, per CNA.
Nvidia had gained more than 30% on Monday after Jensen Huang's reinstatement as CEO.
Hewlett Packard Enterprise fell 13% after weaker margin guidance, Mint reported.
Wednesday's PCE inflation report is the next market focus.
stories.background: Huang resigned less than two weeks ago over reports of extramarital affairs. CNA reported that Nvidia's board reversed course after pressure from President Donald Trump. AI stocks had already sold off through November on worries about profitability and heavy spending. Nvidia remains under scrutiny from investigators, including at the FBI and on Capitol Hill, over allegations it helped Chinese firms access its top chips.
stories.whyItMatters: AI-linked stocks account for a large share of US market value, so swings in Nvidia and its peers move the main indices and Asian chipmakers.

stories.headline: SP names first five UP candidates, two in seats Congress sought
stories.dek: Akhilesh Yadav asked Congress to send a list of other winnable seats and urged both parties to field joint INDIA bloc candidates.
stories.summary: The Samajwadi Party released its first list of five candidates for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh election on Tuesday, two in seats Congress had sought. The SP says it offered Congress 26 seats; Congress denies receiving an offer.
body: The Samajwadi Party on Tuesday night announced its first list of five candidates for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly election, including two constituencies that Congress had sought, while seat-sharing talks with the INDIA bloc ally continued.

The nominees are Umar Ali Khan from Behat, Ashu Malik from Saharanpur, Nahid Hasan from Kairana, Mahboob Ali (spelt Mehboob by NDTV) from Amroha and Jyoti Lodhi from Lalitpur. Hindustan Times said the list has four Muslims and one non-Yadav OBC candidate.

Khan, Malik and Mahboob Ali are sitting SP MLAs. Hasan won the Kairana seat in the 2014 bypoll, 2017 and 2022. Lalitpur is the only seat on the list not held by the SP; the BJP won it in 2017 and 2022.

NDTV, citing sources, reported that Congress had staked a claim to Saharanpur and Behat. It said sources close to Congress leader Imran Masood indicated he would field candidates against the SP in Saharanpur. The Congress was surprised by the announcement, the sources said, and gave no immediate statement.

Shortly before the list appeared, SP president Akhilesh Yadav posted on X asking Congress to send a list of all other seats where it believes it can win, beyond the 26 discussed on Tuesday. He said the two sides would then assess seats and candidates together, and that the SP might point to winnable seats Congress had not considered.

Akhilesh urged that candidates be chosen as INDIA bloc nominees rather than as representatives of two parties, and suggested they be projected as “PDA candidates”. He said both parties' aim was to remove the BJP from power.

On the numbers, the SP's Ram Gopal Yadav said the party offered Congress 26 of 403 seats, including two Congress won in 2022 and four where it finished second. NDTV reported that Congress had submitted a list of around 130 seats, down from an earlier demand of about 180. Scroll reported a figure of 181, citing India Today and Akhilesh.

Congress has denied receiving a formal offer. AICC Uttar Pradesh in-charge Rajendra Pal Gautam said the parties discussed all 403 seats and no specific demands were made, according to PTI. Masood, as quoted by NDTV, asked: “Are we begging the SP for seats?”
Ram Gopal Yadav has said the final allocation is undecided. NDTV reported that two more rounds of talks are expected.

stories.headline: Awami League says Sheikh Hasina plans to return to Bangladesh on December 16
stories.dek: Dhaka says it is discussing the matter only with India, not with Hasina, and a minister told Reuters she would be arrested and jailed on arrival.
stories.summary: Sheikh Hasina's party says the ousted Bangladeshi leader wants to return from India on Victory Day, December 16, and has asked Dhaka for a Biman Bangladesh aircraft. A government adviser said Dhaka is not negotiating with her and is talking to Delhi.
body: Bangladesh's ousted former prime minister, Sheikh Hasina, plans to return home on December 16, Victory Day, her party and spokesperson said, and has asked the government in Dhaka to provide an aircraft for the journey from Delhi.

Hasina's spokesperson, Syed Mozammel Ali, told Reuters that she "calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka", as she had been flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on August 5, 2024. He said it was the government's responsibility to make her return on December 16 possible.

Awami League sources told The Hindu the party had asked for a Biman Bangladesh aircraft but would explore all options, including a land border. A four-member team of senior party leaders, sent on Hasina's instruction, visited Petrapole in West Bengal to assess the Benapole-Petrapole crossing. A party member said other locations, including Agartala-Akhaura and the Siliguri border, would be examined. The sources said Dhaka had not responded to a request for safety and security guarantees.

Dhaka's position is that it will not deal with Hasina directly. Information Adviser Zahed ur Rahman told reporters that whether she returns by air or on foot "is a matter of discussion between us and India. We are not discussing this with Hasina."

An unidentified Bangladeshi minister told Reuters on Sunday that Hasina would be arrested and jailed on return, and that there had been no official talks with India about sending an aircraft. Bangladesh has also stepped up patrols along the Indian border, The Hindu reported.

Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal sentenced Hasina to death in November 2025 for crimes against humanity linked to the 2024 crackdown on protesters. On November 14, Dhaka said it had completed the legal procedures for her return from India and that the extradition decision rests with New Delhi. The Indian government has said it is for Hasina to decide whether to return.

On November 18, Bangladesh deployed hundreds of paramilitary troops after talk of her return was followed by clashes, bomb blasts and arson attacks. The violence has been blamed on supporters of her banned party. The Hindu quoted a senior Indian source as saying India expects more disturbance inside Bangladesh if she tries to return.
Hasina has also asked Dhaka for a new passport and identity card, which the government has so far refused, Scroll reported, citing Reuters.
keyFacts: Hasina wants to return on December 16, Bangladesh's Victory Day, according to her party and spokesperson.
She fled to India on August 5, 2024, after weeks of protests.

stories.whyItMatters: A return attempt could lead to her arrest and, according to Indian and Bangladeshi accounts, further unrest, while testing Dhaka's relations with Delhi over extradition.

stories.headline: Houthi drone strike on Riyadh tower wounds 11, Saudi civil defence says
stories.dek: The Public Investment Fund Tower was reportedly hit for the second time in a week; the Saudi-led coalition called the strike a "terrorist attack".
stories.summary: A Houthi strike on a skyscraper in Riyadh wounded 11 people on Tuesday, Saudi civil defence said. Witnesses told the South China Morning Post the target was the Public Investment Fund Tower, which was also attacked last week.
body: A strike by Yemen's Houthi group on a skyscraper in the Saudi capital Riyadh wounded 11 people on Tuesday, the kingdom's civil defence authority said in a statement.

The wounded were four Egyptian residents, three Nepalese, two Indians and two Saudi citizens, according to the statement, as reported by The New York Times. Al Jazeera and ThePrint, citing Saudi civil defence, also reported 11 injured, and Al Jazeera described the attack as a drone strike.

Saudi authorities did not name the tower that was hit but shared an image of the Public Investment Fund Tower, which houses the sovereign wealth fund, The New York Times reported. The South China Morning Post said three separate witnesses told it the 80-storey tower was the target. The building stands in the King Abdullah Financial District and is the tallest skyscraper in the city, the outlet reported.
The tower was also attacked on Thursday. The Wall Street Journal described Tuesday's strike as the second on the building in under a week.
The coalition fighting the Houthis denounced the attack as a "terrorist attack", according to the South China Morning Post.

The Houthis did not immediately issue a statement or confirm the attack, The New York Times said. The group has repeatedly threatened Riyadh's financial district and has carried out at least two earlier strikes that damaged buildings there, the newspaper reported.
keyFacts: Saudi civil defence said 11 people were wounded on Tuesday.
The injured include four Egyptians, three Nepalese, two Indians and two Saudis.
The Public Investment Fund Tower was also attacked on Thursday.
The Houthis had not confirmed the attack when the reports were published.
stories.background: The Public Investment Fund is the sovereign wealth fund that has played a major role in Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's efforts to project influence abroad, The New York Times reported. The Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia have been exchanging attacks for weeks, the newspaper said.

stories.headline: Rahul Gandhi says Rajiv Gandhi's security was removed on purpose so he would be killed
stories.dek: The Congress leader made the claim in a family video about Sonia Gandhi's book; the SPG Act of 1988 covered only the sitting prime minister.
stories.summary: Rahul Gandhi said in a video with Sonia Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra that his father's security was withdrawn deliberately so he would be killed. The Times of India noted the SPG law then covered only serving prime ministers.
body: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi said the security of his father, former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi, was removed on purpose so that he would be killed, in a video posted on Tuesday with his mother Sonia Gandhi and sister Priyanka Gandhi Vadra.

The three were discussing Sonia Gandhi's recently released book, 'Belonging'. "Papa's security was removed so that he got killed. Papa's security removal was not an accident. It was done on purpose so that he got killed," Rahul Gandhi said, in the wording reported by The Times of India. The Economic Times quoted him as saying "not just an accident".
He added: "An atmosphere was created for him to get killed. It was obvious what was going on. I told papa and mom, and had an argument about it with my father."

His remarks followed Sonia Gandhi's account of Rajiv Gandhi's travel as an opposition leader, including a Bihar visit in 1991 where stones were thrown at him and slogans were raised against him. Rahul Gandhi had accompanied his father. According to Sonia Gandhi, her son told her afterwards: "Mama, if we don't do something about Papa's security, I know I'm going to come back for his funeral very soon."
Rahul Gandhi also said his mother had not written in the book about how some people treated her. He said she was "humiliated, abused" in politics and that he might speak about it someday.

The Times of India said the Special Protection Group Act, passed in 1988 under the Rajiv Gandhi government, limited SPG cover to the serving prime minister and not former prime ministers. Rajiv Gandhi therefore lost that cover after the Congress lost power in 1989, when V P Singh became prime minister.

Rajiv Gandhi was killed by a suicide bomber at an election rally in Sriperumbudur, Tamil Nadu, on May 21, 1991. The Chandra Shekhar government was in office at the time. The P V Narasimha Rao government later amended the Act to cover former prime ministers and their immediate families for five years, and a 1994 amendment extended this to 10 years.

stories.whyItMatters: The remarks reopen the question of who was responsible for Rajiv Gandhi's security after 1989, a matter tied to how protection for former prime ministers and their families was later changed in law.

stories.headline: Putin says Russian retaliation for Ukrainian oil plant strikes is inevitable
stories.dek: Kyiv separately said its naval drone attack on a Russian warship in Libya was self-defence, as a Russian glide bomb attack on Zaporizhzhia killed two people.
stories.summary: President Vladimir Putin said Russia will respond to Ukrainian attacks on its oil refineries. Ukraine's Foreign Ministry defended a strike on a Russian warship in Benghazi, Libya, while a Russian attack on Zaporizhzhia killed two civilians and wounded 48.
body: Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Tuesday that Russia will inevitably respond to Ukrainian attacks on its oil refineries, according to Reuters, Al Jazeera and The Economic Times.

Putin said the government needs to discuss stronger security measures for its energy facilities. He also said US President Donald Trump had asked Ukraine to stop hitting Russian refineries, according to the reports. Al Jazeera reported that Ukrainian attacks on such sites subsided after Trump declared an energy ceasefire in mid-October, but picked up again afterwards.

In Ukraine, a Russian night-time glide bomb attack on Zaporizhzhia killed two civilians and wounded 48, including four children, officials said. Mykhailo Semikin, head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration, said the attack destroyed a private house and partly destroyed a five-storey apartment building. The youngest wounded child was less than a year old, he said. The others were aged 4, 6 and 16.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine is sending reinforcements to the Zaporizhzhia region.

Ukraine also faced questions over a strike on Sunday on a Russian warship docked in Benghazi, in eastern Libya, carried out with naval drones. The Libyan Foreign Ministry said on Monday that the Tripoli-based government had not authorised "any foreign military operations within (Libya's) territory or territorial waters", and asked Ukraine for clarifications. The UN Mission in Libya also expressed concern and said Libya's sovereignty and territorial integrity must be fully respected.

Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi responded on Tuesday that Ukraine intended no harm to Libya or its people. "Ukraine's actions are directed solely against [Russia] and not against any third party," he said. He argued that international law does not limit the right of self-defence to the place where aggression occurs, and that Russia uses civilian infrastructure in third countries for military purposes. Reuters summarised Kyiv's position as self-defence.

Russia's Defence Ministry said its air defences intercepted 699 Ukrainian drones overnight over several Russian regions, Crimea and the Black Sea. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said about half were heading towards the Moscow region. Flights at Vnukovo and Sheremetyevo airports were restricted for several hours, according to Rosaviatsia.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine needs 115 billion euros ($126 billion) in foreign aid next year. He said 90 billion euros is already assured, leaving 25 billion euros to find.

stories.background: Russia and Ukraine have stepped up aerial strikes in recent months while taking part in US-mediated talks to end the war, which began with Russia's full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022. Russian bombardments aim to knock out Ukraine's power supply before winter, while Ukraine has hit targets as far away as Siberia.
stories.whyItMatters: Putin's pledge points to further Russian strikes after Ukraine's attacks on energy sites, while the Libya strike has drawn Libyan and UN concern over sovereignty.

stories.headline: Indians among 13 killed in bus-truck collision in UAE's Ras Al Khaimah
stories.dek: The Indian consulate in Dubai said it has contacted families and opened a 24-hour helpline, but the number of Indian victims has not been confirmed.
stories.summary: A passenger bus carrying 41 people hit a truck on Al Watan Road in Ras Al Khaimah, killing 13 and injuring 14. The Indian consulate in Dubai said Indian nationals were among the dead.
body: At least 13 people were killed and 14 injured on Tuesday when a passenger bus collided with a truck on Al Watan Road in the UAE's Ras Al Khaimah, and the Indian consulate in Dubai said Indian nationals were among the dead.

The bus was carrying 41 people. It crashed into a truck that was stopped at the roadside after a mechanical fault, according to the Khaleej Times and local authorities cited by The Times of India. The Times of India reported that the crash took place in the early hours.

The UAE Ministry of Interior first reported 11 deaths. The toll rose to 13 after two injured passengers died in hospital, Gulf News reported. Rescue teams took the injured to nearby hospitals, according to The Times of India, which said their injuries varied in severity.

The consulate said in a post on X that it was "deeply saddened" by the accident and had reached out to the bereaved families. It said it was working closely with local authorities to provide "all possible assistance and support" and that further details were being ascertained.
The number of Indians killed or injured has not been confirmed. The consulate has set up a 24-hour toll-free helpline, 800-46342, for people seeking information or help.

The crash came less than two weeks after a multi-vehicle collision in Fujairah on November 13. It involved 23 vehicles, including trucks, and killed 14 people, four of them Indian nationals. About 30 people were injured, including seven Indians.

stories.headline: Passport office notice over birthplace behind CJP's Saurav Das being stopped at Delhi airport
stories.dek: The Chennai Regional Passport Office gave Das seven days to explain his place of birth; he says he saw the emailed notice only after immigration stopped him.
stories.summary: Cockroach Janta Party co-convenor Saurav Das was stopped at Delhi airport on a London flight after a Chennai passport office notice flagged his place of birth. Das denies any discrepancy and says the government has "lost the plot"; the government has issued no statement.
body: Saurav Das, co-convenor of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), was stopped at Delhi's Indira Gandhi International Airport late on Monday from boarding a flight to London after the Regional Passport Office (RPO) in Chennai flagged his passport over an alleged discrepancy in his place of birth.

The RPO emailed Das a show-cause notice at 7.30 pm on November 23, hours before his flight, which was due to leave at 1 am on November 24. The notice, seen by The Hindu, said inputs indicated that the place of birth in his August 8, 2019 passport application was incorrect and that the passport, dated August 21, 2019, was "obtained by material suppression of facts". It gave him seven days to respond with supporting documents and said failure to do so could lead to impounding under Section 10(3)(b) of the Passports Act, 1967. It advised him not to use the passport until he replied.

A senior government official told The Hindu there appeared to be a mismatch in his date of birth, place of birth and father's name across his Aadhaar, birth certificate and passport. The official said Das did not respond to the RPO, after which the passport was flagged. The government has issued no official statement. The BBC said it had asked the home ministry, Delhi police and airport officials for comment.

Das said he saw the email only after immigration officers stopped him and told him to check it. He said no problem was raised when the passport was issued in 2019 after police verification, and that he had travelled abroad twice since. He said he would respond to the notice. "I will comply with any lawful inquiry. But if you do CAA-NRC in the garb of an inquiry, I will not allow that," he said.

Das told the BBC there were no discrepancies in his documents and that the government had "completely lost the plot". He said he was to speak at the Oxford Union and at events at institutions including Cambridge, the London School of Economics (LSE), Edinburgh and Queen Mary. The Indian Express noted the invitation was from the Oxford Union, a debating society independent of the University of Oxford. The LSE Student Union's Amnesty International Unit said on Instagram on Tuesday that an event featuring Das had been "indefinitely postponed", the BBC reported.

CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke asked, "Is Saurav a criminal? Has he looted a bank?" He compared the case with that of Vijay Mallya, Nirav Modi and Mehul Choksi. CJP leader Ratna Singh said the episode raised "deeply troubling questions" about freedom of expression.

The notice followed a September 30 Madras High Court order on a public interest petition by Chennai businessman R. Ganesh Kumar. The petition seeks a Union Home Ministry inquiry into Das's nationality and cancellation of his passport and Aadhaar if he is found not to be an Indian. The court issued notice to Das.
The RPO notice gives Das until about November 30 to respond, based on its seven-day period.

stories.background: The CJP began as satire and became a youth-led pressure group. Protests it led over exam paper leaks preceded Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation on July 25. In October, Das was detained with other CJP leaders on arrival in Delhi and later jailed for seven days after an arrest for trespassing at a banned protest site, the BBC reported.
stories.whyItMatters: Das's passport faces possible impounding if his reply to the notice is found unsatisfactory, and his planned UK engagements have been disrupted.

stories.headline: China places Shanghai party chief and Politburo member Chen Jining under investigation
stories.dek: Chen, 62, had been widely tipped for a senior national post at the Communist Party Congress due next year, according to The Hindu and The New York Times.
stories.summary: China's state news agency announced on Tuesday that Shanghai party secretary Chen Jining is under investigation for suspected serious violations of discipline and law. Chen, a Politburo member, had been widely seen as headed for a higher role under Xi Jinping.
body: China announced on Tuesday that Chen Jining, the Communist Party secretary of Shanghai and a member of the Politburo, is under investigation for suspected serious violations of discipline and the law.

The announcement came in a brief bulletin from Xinhua, the official news agency, which gave no details of the allegations. According to The Hindu, Chen is being investigated by the party's Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and the National Commission of Supervision. The New York Times noted that the phrase used usually refers to allegations of corruption.

Chen, 62, trained as an environmental scientist and did his doctoral studies in environmental engineering at Imperial College London. He was president of Tsinghua University, President Xi Jinping's alma mater, and later minister for environmental protection. He was mayor of Beijing from 2018 to 2022 and has led the party in Shanghai since 2022.

The Hindu reported that Chen was popular with foreign business representatives in Shanghai and was among the few top party leaders with significant international exposure. Both the Times and The Hindu said he had widely been expected to move to a higher post. The Hindu said he was tipped for a prominent national role at the Party Congress held once every five years, due next year, when Xi is expected to begin a fourth term.

Politburo members are rarely investigated, The Hindu reported. It said only about half a dozen members at that level have been removed in the past three decades, often in the run-up to a Party Congress. Previous Shanghai party secretaries have often risen to the Politburo Standing Committee, the Times noted.

Under Xi, several Politburo-ranked figures have been removed, including former security chief Zhou Yongkang and former Chongqing party secretary Sun Zhengcai. The Hindu said that earlier this year PLA generals Zhang Youxia and He Weidong were removed, along with former Xinjiang party secretary Ma Xingrui. It said Chen would be the fourth member of the current Politburo to be placed under investigation.

Chen attended the party's Fifth Plenum in Beijing last month, The Hindu reported. That meeting confirmed the expulsion of as many as 33 Central Committee members, including 16 PLA generals, and ended with a pledge to "persevere with full and rigorous party self-governance".

stories.whyItMatters: The investigation removes a leading candidate for a senior national post ahead of the 2027 Party Congress and leaves Shanghai, a major commercial city, without its party chief.

stories.headline: Kuki and Naga leaders agree to peace process in Manipur, urge Christmas truce
stories.dek: The Forum for Naga Reconciliation said both sides will hold another round of dialogue before Christmas, with all stakeholders invited.
stories.summary: Kuki and Naga Christian and civil society leaders said on Tuesday they had agreed to begin a process to address the causes of conflict in Manipur. The Forum for Naga Reconciliation, which organised the Kolkata summit, asked both communities to work towards a Christmas truce.
body: Kuki and Naga leaders representing Christian and civil society groups said on Tuesday they had agreed to begin a "forward-looking" process to identify and address the problems fuelling conflict between the two communities in Manipur.

The agreement came at the Kuki-Naga Prayer and Peace Summit, held in Kolkata from Sunday to Tuesday and organised by the Forum for Naga Reconciliation. The forum said it was asking both communities to "work towards a Christmas truce".

In a statement, the forum said the leaders had "engaged in an honest, open-spirited and respectful dialogue" and "recognised and acknowledged how deeply they have hurt one another". They also recognised the need to explore ways to "break the chain of fear, hate and violence", it said.

Kuki groups at the summit were Kuki Christian Churches Manipur, Kuki Baptist Churches Manipur, Kuki Inpi Manipur, Kuki Christian Leader's Forum, Kuki Baptist Association Nagaland and Kuki Christian Church Nagaland. The Naga side was represented by the Naga Christian Forum Manipur, Naga Peoples' Initiative for Peace Manipur, Fellowship of Naga Baptist Association and the United Naga Council.

The forum said the truce should serve as a confidence-building measure. It should create conditions for immediate relief to affected families and "end the cycle of violence and prevent further escalation and the loss of human lives". It would also let community leaders begin "real dialogue around the underlying core issues of the conflict", the forum said.

"The leaders are fully aware that the road to peace is not a quick-fix, but one that requires political and moral courage and willingness to be part of a sustained and broader dialogue to peace," the statement said.

The summit also appealed to people to "stop the violence of words waged through" social media. "The lies, rumours, hatred and propaganda are instilling more animosity and polarisation. This must end immediately," the forum said.
To consolidate the process, the leaders agreed to hold another round of dialogue before Christmas, to which all stakeholders would be invited.
keyFacts: The Kuki-Naga Prayer and Peace Summit was held in Kolkata from Sunday to Tuesday.
The Forum for Naga Reconciliation organised the summit and asked for a Christmas truce.
The toll in Kuki-Naga clashes in Manipur since February is 72, according to Scroll.
Another round of dialogue is planned before Christmas, with all stakeholders invited.
stories.background:
Tensions between the Kuki and Naga communities have escalated in Manipur since February. The conflict flared after ethnic clashes between the Meitei and Kuki-Zo-Hmar communities began in May 2023.

More than 300 people have been killed and 49 are missing since May 2023, the Assembly was informed in September. About 60,000 were displaced; 36,000 have been resettled and 24,000 remain in relief camps.
stories.whyItMatters: The truce appeal seeks immediate relief for families affected by the Kuki-Naga clashes, which have killed 72 people since February.

stories.headline: Israeli strikes kill seven in Gaza, including Hamas internal security chief
stories.dek: Israel's military said it killed Naeem Abu Nahel, who took the post in September after his predecessor was captured, as the October 2025 ceasefire remains in place.
stories.summary: Israeli air strikes in Gaza on Tuesday killed seven people, including Hamas internal security chief Naeem Abu Nahel, health officials and Israel said. Hamas-run authorities called the strikes part of a campaign against Gaza's police.
body: Israeli air strikes in Gaza on Tuesday killed seven people, including Naeem Abu Nahel, head of Hamas's internal security service, Palestinian officials and the Israeli military said, despite a ceasefire that took effect in October 2025.

Gaza's Hamas-run interior ministry said Abu Nahel, 50, was targeted in western Gaza City. Witnesses told the BBC an Israeli drone hit him as he walked along a side street near a tent camp for displaced people. Mahmoud Bassal, spokesman for Gaza's civil defence agency, told AFP several other people were in critical condition after that strike.

The Israeli military, in a joint statement with the Shin Bet security agency, said it had "eliminated" Abu Nahel, whom it named as Naim Muhammad Ashour Abu Nahal. It said he had held the post for two months. It alleged he had advanced attacks on Israeli troops and civilians during the war, and said his death was "a blow to the apparatus's management capabilities".
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz congratulated security forces, saying "no terrorist will escape the long arm" of Israel.

The other six deaths came in two earlier strikes, according to health officials and first responders. Three people, including a teenage boy reported by The Hindu to be 17, were killed in the Wadi Gaza area, south of Gaza City. Three more died at a police station in al-Mawasi, west of Khan Younis.

Gaza's police force said two of its officers, aged 23 and 33, were among the dead at the police station. It described the attack as part of "an ongoing campaign targeting the police apparatus aimed at sowing chaos". The Israeli military said it struck "military operatives" in both areas, though The Hindu reported it did not confirm the strike that killed the teenager.
Gaza's interior ministry said Abu Nahel's killing followed what it called the security service's achievements against gangs collaborating with Israel.
Abu Nahel took over in September after his predecessor was captured in a raid by Israeli special forces, the BBC reported.

The Gaza health ministry says at least 1,679 people have been killed since the ceasefire began; an AFP tally puts the figure above 1,650. Israel says six soldiers have been killed in that period, according to the BBC, while The Hindu, citing the Israeli military, reported seven soldiers and one civilian contractor.

Cogat, the Israeli military body overseeing aid, said on Monday it was working on a humanitarian response, including a newly approved package of pumps, generators, water tankers and medical equipment. Gaza's health ministry said on Tuesday that 272 meningitis cases were reported in October, about eight times the usual monthly average.
keyFacts: Seven people were killed in three Israeli strikes in Gaza on Tuesday, November 24.
Naeem Abu Nahel, 50, had led Hamas's internal security service since September.
Two police officers, aged 23 and 33, died in the al-Mawasi strike, Gaza police said.
The Gaza health ministry says at least 1,679 people have died since the October 2025 ceasefire.
Israel's military says it controls more than 60 percent of Gaza.
stories.background: Israel and Hamas agreed a US-brokered ceasefire in October 2025, after two years of war that began with the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage. Both sides regularly accuse each other of violations, and Israeli strikes occur almost daily. Gaza's health ministry says more than 74,740 people have been killed in Gaza since the war began; the UN considers its figures reliable.
stories.whyItMatters: Most of Gaza's 2.1 million people live displaced in tents or makeshift shelters, and continued strikes coincide with flooding damage, winter supply needs and a rise in meningitis cases.

perspectives.summary: The military and Shin Bet said Abu Nahel was a long-standing Hamas member who advanced attacks on Israelis, and that killing him removed a threat and weakened the apparatus's management.

perspectives.summary: Gaza's police and interior ministry describe the strikes as a campaign against the police apparatus meant to sow chaos, and say the security service had been countering gangs collaborating with Israel.

stories.headline: Gunmen hold hostages in Cartagena supermarket after failed armoured-car robbery
stories.dek: President Abelardo de la Espriella said the hostage-takers are common criminals, not an armed group, and that some of those held have been freed.
stories.summary: Masked gunmen who tried to rob an armoured vehicle took hostages in an Éxito supermarket in Cartagena on Tuesday. Reports differ on the number held, and local media said at least 15 people had been released by the evening.
body: Armed and masked men took people hostage in an Éxito supermarket in the Colombian tourist city of Cartagena on Tuesday after an apparent failed attempt to rob an armoured cash-in-transit vehicle, President Abelardo de la Espriella said.

The gunmen arrived at about 8.30am local time at the store in the La Castellana neighbourhood, according to The Guardian. The president said they planned to rob a vehicle due to collect the previous day's takings. Employees spotted the movement on security cameras and alerted police, who surrounded the building.

The number held is reported differently. De la Espriella said 30 people were initially taken hostage and five, described as older women, were released. France 24, quoting the president, put the number still held at 25. The Guardian, citing Caracol Radio, reported that another 10 were later freed. No injuries had been reported, The Guardian said.

Images broadcast by Colombian media showed masked gunmen with rifles standing beside hostages who appeared to be kneeling on the floor. Police snipers took positions on nearby buildings and streets were sealed off. Special forces were deployed, and city authorities said the navy and army were also involved.

Local media reported that the gunmen were demanding nearly $2 million, two armoured vehicles and safe passage to Barranquilla, about 130 kilometres to the northeast. AFP said it could not verify the reports.
Rafael Nuñez International Airport briefly suspended landings while the armed forces used a runway in connection with the operation. Landings resumed about 45 minutes later, according to France 24.

De la Espriella spoke from Villavicencio, where he was dealing with a car bomb attack on Monday night outside the Meta departmental government headquarters. He ruled out the involvement of armed groups in Cartagena. "It's not that a terrorist group carried out a kidnapping -- no, these are criminals who were caught off guard, had no way out, and then kidnapped a group of people," he said.
He added: "This is going to turn out well for the hostages. I'm not so sure it's going to turn out so well for the criminals."
Jacob Perez, whose son works at the supermarket, told AFP: "My son is there. He didn't leave work and he's not answering his phone. I think they took it from him."
keyFacts: Gunmen entered an Éxito supermarket in La Castellana, Cartagena, at about 8.30am on Tuesday.
President De la Espriella said 30 were first taken hostage and five older women were released.
Caracol Radio reported another 10 hostages were later freed.
Local media said the gunmen demanded nearly $2 million; AFP could not verify this.
Cartagena airport suspended landings for about 45 minutes.
stories.background: The incident followed a car bomb on Monday night outside the Meta departmental government headquarters in Villavicencio. That attack killed a security guard and wounded more than 20 people, and the president blamed a dissident Farc faction. Early on Monday, drones believed to be flown by the ELN hit homes in Cúcuta, injuring three civilians. De la Espriella has been in office just over three months.
stories.whyItMatters: Cartagena draws hundreds of thousands of visitors a year, and the siege disrupted air travel and a residential area of the city.

stories.headline: Police stop Mehbooba Mufti at Chandanwari on way to Sheshnag lake
stories.dek: The PDP president was headed to see BRO work near the glacial lake, which the agency says is widening and stabilisation of the Amarnath yatra track.
stories.summary: Police stopped PDP president Mehbooba Mufti at Chandanwari on Tuesday as she tried to reach Sheshnag lake, where a video of an excavator has caused a row. The Border Roads Organisation says it is widening the existing yatra track.
body: Police stopped Peoples Democratic Party president Mehbooba Mufti at Chandanwari on Tuesday as she tried to trek to Sheshnag lake, about 12 km away, to see construction work by the Border Roads Organisation (BRO) on the Amarnath yatra route.
The Indian Express reported that police cited "security reasons". Two PDP legislators, Waheed Para and Aga Muntazir Mehdi, were with her.

"My worst fears were confirmed today when police stopped me from proceeding towards Sheshnag," Mufti said, according to The Times of India. She added: "What is being concealed today could become a man-made disaster tomorrow."

The row began after a video circulated showing an excavator moving earth near the lake, which lies on the Pahalgam-Amarnath cave trekking route. The Indian Express reported that the video was first posted by an Instagram account, which later deleted it.

The BRO said the circulating video's claim of new works was incorrect. In a statement, it said it had begun widening tracks and stabilising vulnerable stretches, based on experience of the previous yatra and a need for a wider road, to ease congestion and allow safer passage. It said measures were in place for safe disposal of excavated material and to protect natural drainage.

Political and religious figures and environmental activists have called for work with heavy machinery to stop. Mirwaiz Umar Farooq called the visuals "very disturbing". CPI(M) leader M Y Tarigami said the government must stop any work that threatens the lake. Climate activist Raja Muzaffar Bhat said more people should approach the Supreme Court, the National Green Tribunal or the high court.

Hasnian Masoodi, a National Conference MLA, rejected the BRO's explanation. "If the track is being made safer, why are earthmovers being taken over there?" he said. Congress MP Pawan Khera said on Monday that Sheshnag is not a construction site.

The BJP defended the work. State spokesperson Girdhari Lal Raina said some political elements had found a new pretext to communalise the matter, and that the work concerns widening and stabilisation of the existing Chandanwari-Amarnath track.
keyFacts: Police stopped Mehbooba Mufti at Chandanwari, about 12 km from Sheshnag lake, on Tuesday.
Waheed Para and Aga Muntazir Mehdi, both PDP MLAs, accompanied her.
The BRO says it is widening and stabilising the existing Amarnath yatra track.
Sheshnag is among 14 high-risk glacial lakes identified in Jammu & Kashmir, The Times of India reported.
stories.background: Sheshnag is a glacial lake on the route to the Amarnath cave and is considered sacred in Hinduism. The Times of India reported that it is the source of the Lidder river. Activists describe the surrounding terrain as steep slopes and glacial deposits.
stories.whyItMatters: The dispute concerns work on a route used by Amarnath pilgrims and an ecologically sensitive lake that feeds the Lidder river.

perspectives.label: PDP, opposition and activists
perspectives.summary: They say heavy machinery threatens a fragile glacial ecosystem and a sacred lake, and want work halted. Mufti said the questions about construction are growing louder.

perspectives.label: BRO and BJP
perspectives.summary: The BRO says it is widening and stabilising the existing track for pilgrim safety with environmental safeguards. The BJP accuses critics of communalising the issue.

stories.headline: 20 rebel TMC MPs tell Speaker Om Birla their move to NCPI broke no rules
stories.dek: The replies, each 17-18 pages, answer disqualification petitions filed by Abhishek Banerjee and were submitted on the last day of the Lok Sabha Secretariat's deadline.
stories.summary: The 20 rebel Trinamool Congress MPs who joined the NCPI have filed replies to Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla, saying they followed constitutional norms. The Speaker must now examine the responses to Abhishek Banerjee's disqualification petitions.
body: The 20 rebel Trinamool Congress MPs who joined the Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI) submitted replies to Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla on Tuesday, saying their exit from the TMC violated no parliamentary or constitutional provision.

The replies were filed on the last day of the deadline set by the Lok Sabha Secretariat. They answer petitions by TMC national general secretary Abhishek Banerjee seeking the MPs' disqualification under the anti-defection law.

Kakoli Ghosh Dastidar, who leads the NCPI group in Parliament, said each MP sent an individual reply of 17-18 pages. "We have joined the NCPI following all parliamentary and constitutional norms," she told PTI. The Indian Express describes her as NCPI parliamentary chairperson; The Hindu calls her chief whip.

NCPI MP Arup Chakraborty said the breakaway was a collective decision taken after the TMC lost the West Bengal Assembly elections. "We felt that if we had to sustain our organisation and retain people's respect, we needed to form a team," he said.

Chakraborty said the decision to back the BJP-led NDA came later. He rejected the charge of anti-party activity. "We believe this is not an issue, as we are the majority group, and hope that the majority's position will be recognised," he said. Sudip Bandyopadhyay, leader of the NCPI bloc in the Lok Sabha, said the replies rebutted Banerjee's allegations.

Asked about the repeated delays, Chakraborty cited festivals including Bhai Phonta, Kali Puja, Diwali and Durga Puja. The MPs had sought extensions five times, saying they needed to collate documents and prepare replies with their legal team. He also said a meeting with Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari could not be ruled out.

The TMC leadership says the rebels cannot escape the consequences of leaving the party by describing it as a political realignment. Party leader Kunal Ghosh had earlier criticised the extension requests, calling the MPs "turncoats, opportunists and ungrateful people".

The Hindu reported that the Supreme Court agreed on August 25 to hear Banerjee's plea for an expeditious decision by the Speaker. Whether a collective departure is protected under the Tenth Schedule will have to be examined, the paper said. The Speaker will now go through the replies and arguments from both sides.
keyFacts: 20 of the TMC's 27 Lok Sabha MPs joined the NCPI, according to The Hindu.
Each rebel MP filed a reply of 17-18 pages on Tuesday, November 24.
The Lok Sabha Secretariat issued notices on August 26; the MPs sought five extensions.

stories.background:
The split began in June, when 20 of the TMC's 27 Lok Sabha MPs broke away after the party's defeat in the West Bengal Assembly elections and extended support to the NDA. Official Lok Sabha records still list them as TMC MPs, The Hindu reported.

The division extends to the state Assembly, where around 60 of 80 TMC MLAs backed Ritabrata Banerjee's claim to the Leader of the Opposition's post. The Election Commission allotted the name Mamata All India Trinamool Congress to the Mamata Banerjee faction and Democratic Trinamool Congress to the rival group.
stories.whyItMatters: The Speaker's decision on the petitions will determine whether the 20 MPs keep their Lok Sabha seats and whether their group gains recognition as a separate parliamentary formation.

stories.headline: Anthropic shares close below $83 IPO price, four days after Nasdaq debut
stories.dek: The stock has fallen about 31% from its peak, wiping out close to $200 billion in value, though several brokerages began coverage with buy-equivalent ratings.
stories.summary: Anthropic shares closed 6.5% lower on Tuesday, below the $83 offer price, four days after the company's record Nasdaq debut. Analysts at Canaccord Genuity, Wedbush and Oppenheimer initiated coverage with positive ratings.
body: Shares of Anthropic, the developer of the Claude AI models, closed down 6.5% on Tuesday, falling below the $83 price at which the company sold stock in its initial public offering (IPO), CNBC reported.

The stock opened at $111.50 on the Nasdaq on Thursday, November 19, and has declined steadily since. Reuters said the fall puts the company on track to lose nearly $200 billion in value. The Wall Street Journal said Tuesday was the third straight session of losses.

During the day, TechCrunch reported the shares traded as low as $76, nearly 12% below Monday's close. Mint reported an intraday low of $79.42 after the shares opened at $83.40. Mint put the fall at 31% from the record high of $111.53, when the company's market value was close to $2 trillion. It later retreated to around $1 trillion, Mint said.

The offering was the largest on record. CNBC said Anthropic raised $81.3 billion. Mint, citing Bloomberg, said demand exceeded $500 billion, and that the haul rose to $93.5 billion after underwriters bought additional shares. The sources give different totals. The previous record was SpaceX's $85.7 billion listing in June.
CNBC reported that roughly half of the institutional investors who placed orders received no shares. It said those firms did not appear to be buying during the decline.

Other AI-linked stocks also fell on Tuesday. Chipmakers Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Intel, and neoclouds (companies that rent out computing power for AI) CoreWeave, IREN and Nebius, all declined during the session. Nvidia shares rose more than 30% on Monday after the company reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, then gave back part of the gain on Tuesday.

Analysts remained largely positive. Canaccord Genuity began coverage with a buy rating and a $135 price target. It said risks were "unusually large, particularly around infrastructure commitments and the durability of competitive differentiation". Oppenheimer set an outperform rating and a $150 target. Wedbush, on Monday, set an outperform rating and a $120 target.

TechCrunch said that trading below the offer price is often read as a negative signal, and that a prolonged slump could weigh on private AI startup valuations and on the listing plans of other AI companies. Mint listed potential insider selling, competition from open-weight AI models and a possible slowdown in data-centre spending among the near-term risks.
Mint also reported that OpenAI has filed confidentially for a public listing but does not plan to go public before 2027.
keyFacts: Anthropic closed down 6.5% on Tuesday, below its $83 IPO price.
Shares opened at $111.50 on Nasdaq on November 19.
Canaccord set a $135 target; Wedbush $120; Oppenheimer $150.
SpaceX took about a month to fall below its $85.7 billion IPO's offer price, per Mint.

stories.background: An IPO is the first sale of a company's shares to public investors. Underwriters, the banks that run the sale, typically price shares at a discount to their expected trading value, according to TechCrunch. Anthropic is widely seen as a proxy for the AI sector, Mint said, as the first company building frontier (most advanced) AI models to go public.
stories.whyItMatters: Venture capitalists and other observers are treating Anthropic's trading as a gauge of how public investors value AI companies, according to TechCrunch. A weak run could affect private startup valuations and other AI listings.

stories.headline: SpiceJet cuts to about 20 daily flights as operating fleet falls to six aircraft
stories.dek: Promoter Ajay Singh met Civil Aviation Ministry officials on Monday, days after the DGCA issued a show-cause notice over cancellations and alleged violations.
stories.summary: SpiceJet is operating a little over 20 flights a day with six aircraft, sources told The Hindu businessline. Promoter Ajay Singh briefed Civil Aviation Ministry officials on Monday as passenger grievances against the airline rose.
body: SpiceJet is now operating a little over 20 flights a day with a fleet of six aircraft, sources told The Hindu businessline, as the airline's operations shrank further.
Promoter Ajay Singh met Ministry of Civil Aviation officials on Monday to update them on the airline's situation, according to the sources. The ministry has not been quoted in the reports reviewed.

The operational fleet comprises two Q400 turboprops and four Boeing 737 NG aircraft, the sources said. The airline is flying a limited set of services, including Delhi–Mumbai, Delhi–Srinagar, Delhi–Dharamshala, Patna and Darbhanga, among other routes.

The Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) issued a show-cause notice to the airline on November 17. It sought detailed responses on rising flight cancellations, operational disruptions linked to delayed payments, and alleged regulatory violations. SpiceJet was given seven days to respond.

Passenger complaints have also risen. The ministry's AirSewa dashboard listed 8,671 grievances against SpiceJet in data dated November 22, the latest available. The dashboard showed 7,674 grievances in data dated November 19.

Bloomberg, in a report headlined "India's Holiday Travelers Face Another Airline Crisis", framed the airline's reduced operations as a problem for holiday-season travellers. Its full text was not available for this report.
